en: The Āśvamedhika Parva (The Book of the Horse Sacrifice)
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men, as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī and Vyāsa, one should then utter the word "Victory! (Jayam).
When the moon of fame had vanished and the sun-like Bhīṣma had set,
the son of Dharma fell down, his lotus-face withered by grief.
While he was despondent along with his kinsmen, overwhelmed by a swoon of delusion,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra steadied his grief and slowly spoke to him.
Arise, O protector of the earth! You ought not to abandon your fortitude;
you have heard from the sages concerning the essence-less course of saṃsāra.
This is no occasion for grief for you, who have not fallen away from your own duty;
protect [us], O ocean of the nectar of sentient beings, like Prajāpati protects his subjects.
This very time is now appropriate for me alone to grieve,
since I did not listen to Vidura’s words, which were radiant with sound policy.
When Dhṛtarāṣṭra had spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa addressed the king:
"Do not grieve; enjoy this earth obtained through the duty of a kṣatriya."
For prosperity, which depends upon fortitude, flees from those who suffer;
therefore, O King, being victorious, perform sacrifice to dispel the fear of sin.

"By means of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) according to the prescribed rite, you have attained the fitness for it. Having heard these words of the sage, he set his heart's desire upon the sacrifice.
Considering that ritual action is rooted in wealth,
he then, eager for the sacrifice, summoned all the treasury officials and reflected upon the royal treasury.
From them he heard that his entire property had been destroyed by the Kauravas in battle,
and that he was hopeless regarding the horse sacrifice due to his lack of wealth.
Vyāsa, an ocean of compassion, spoke as if to soothe King Marutta regarding the remnants of his sacrifice on the Himalayas.
"Abundant gold exists; you shall obtain it for the sake of the sacrifice.
Having heard this from the son of Pāṇḍu, [the king spoke] to King Marutta. (Bhājana 14.13)
Questioned regarding the discourse on the great sacrifices, that bull among sages,
a treasury of the glories of the great in the illustrious lineage of Manu, spoke.
In the lineage of Karaṃdhama, there was a glorious king named Marutta;
Indra constantly vied with him, yet he could not equal him in his deeds.
Then, tormented by resentment, he spoke privately to Bṛhaspati:
"The lord of the earth, Karaṃdhama, became the patron for whom your father performed sacrifices."
In due course, his son Marutta appeared, who surpassed him in virtues;
however, because of the rivalry arising from his pride, I make this request of you.
"You must not now go to the position of his priest.
Thus requested by Maghavan, Bṛhaspati replied, "So be it."
"From this day forward, no mortal shall be my patron for sacrifice"— with this resolve,
in the meantime, King Marutta prepared a vast sacrificial rite.
Having resolved to perform the sacrifice, he approached Bṛhaspati;
entreated by him with great effort, [Bṛhaspati said], "May you be the officiating priest."
Restrained by the entreaties of Śakra, he did not grant his consent;
having been rejected by his preceptor, the king stood with his face bowed in shame.
Proceeding with his resolve shattered, he saw Nārada on the path;
Nārada, too, having beheld him, questioned him, and heard his story.
He said: "O King, abandon your distress; do not be despondent.
There is a treasure of splendors called Saṃvarta, the younger brother of Bṛhaspati."
That lord of yogins, who moves according to his own will, resides in Vārāṇasī;
he is to be known as Saṃvarta—go to him for refuge.
When asked, "By whom was I announced? you, having bowed to him, should say: "Nārada informed me that you were staying here."
Having spoken thus with great joy to the blazing fire,
that best of sacrificers should address the officiating priest as follows.
When Nārada had spoken thus, the king, overflowing with joy,
went to Vārāṇasī himself and performed everything exactly as he had been told.
Having abandoned his mad appearance and approached that officiating priest, the king,
with the priest's permission, performed austerities on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain.
Having propitiated the god Śaṅkara through austerity, that king, desiring wealth for his sacrifices,
obtained gold as vast as many Mount Merus.
Then, as all the vessels were fashioned out of gold by artisans,
the monarch’s preparations for the sacrifice proceeded in full abundance.
Having learned of his incomparable prosperity at the sacrifice, Bṛhaspati became distressed upon seeing Saṃvartaka as the officiating priest and grew thin.
Questioned by Śakra regarding the cause of his grief, he, with a dejected mind and agitated by rivalry with his brother, spoke of the splendor of Marutta’s sacrifice.
Then Śatakratu, who is devoted to his preceptor, desiring to please him, summoned Agni and said: "Go to King Marutta."
Having gone there, you must speak to that king on my behalf at the sacrifice,
so that he may abandon Saṃvartaka and become the patron of Bṛhaspati.
Thus addressed by the king of the gods, Agni went to the lord of men and delivered Śakra’s message, but the king did not accept it.
Then, having returned, the Fire-god, trembling with fear at the time of universal dissolution, was urged again by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt to go forth, and he spoke:
There, while he was living as a religious student, Saṃvartaka, a mass of splendor, spoke to me in anger: "I would curse you if you were to come here again."
Having heard this, Purandara said to him, "Are you afraid?
Then Agni, blazing with the sacrificial oblation of his wrath, replied to him.
"Alas! O Śakra, has the fire of Brahmā’s wrath against you—the beloved of Ahalyā—been forgotten by you through negligence, anger, or delusion?"
When Cyavana, out of anger, created the fierce and great-tusked Mahāsura for the sake of your destruction, where had your fortitude gone then?
"The wrath of a brahmin is unbearable; it consumes the world in an instant," said the Fire-god, yet [the king] was unable to say anything in reply.
Released once more by Indra, the lord of the Gandharvas said to the king,
"Worship your preceptor," but the king did not accept him.
Then the wielder of the thunderbolt himself, enraged and roaring with a deep sound,
went through the sky, surrounded by clouds, to the sacrificial ground of the king.
Then, by the great power of Saṃvarta of fierce splendor,
the thunderbolt discharged by Śatamanyu entered the clouds.
Then, summoned helplessly by the power of that mantra, the slayer of Vṛtra arrived together with the gods who are entitled to their shares and who drink the soma.
Then, honored by Marutta, Śatakratu, his anger appeased,
became intent on serving the preparations for the sacrificial rite.
By his command, all the gods, for a long time, became subject to the king's instructions and prepared the materials for the sacrifice.
Thus, by the power of King Indrajit’s merit,
the sacrifice of that showerer of gold reached its completion without any obstacle.
"By means of the wealth remaining from that, you shall, being self-restrained, attain the great horse sacrifice (aśvamedha)";
having said this, the lord of sages fell silent.

***** The Chapter on Saṃvarta and Marutta ***** Then Yudhiṣṭhira, being exhorted by Kṛṣṇa as well as by his brothers who were sages, regained his fortitude as he resolved upon the horse sacrifice. BhmJ 14.50.
Then, as the son of Dharma proceeded to attend to the affairs of his subjects,
that entire circle of sages vanished after taking their leave of him.
Then, in the assembly garden, which was as lovely as a creeper of gold and jewels and featured blooming golden lotuses, the two Kṛṣṇas sported at their ease with joy.
At the conclusion of their conversation, the beloved of Subhadrā said to the enemy of Kaṃsa:
"Everything that you spoke at the commencement of the battle has been forgotten by me."
"O knower of the ultimate truth, let that knowledge which was previously imparted be told again.
Thus addressed by the son of Pāṇḍu, the despondent Keśava spoke.
"Alas! Because you lack discernment, you did not listen with attention;
it cannot be said again, yet even so, let this be heard."

In former times, a certain perfected one who had attained the state of liberation while living was questioned by a brahmin; having realized the delusion of worldly existence, he explained everything to him.
In this unreal aggregate of beings composed of the five elements,
the living soul (jīva), bound by the qualities (guṇas), remains like a bird in a cage.
For embodied beings whose sole essence is egoism and who have forgotten their true self,
the decline and rise of pleasure and pain revolve like a wheel.
At the end of the body, due to the connection with their karma— whether through auspicious or evil deeds—
living beings resort to celestial chariots in the form of stars, or to the hells.
Then, upon the exhaustion of his enjoyments,
the self— consisting of the form of semen and immersed in blood— enters the womb, enveloped by the fetal membrane.
Just as water vanishes from the surface of a mirror by the tips of one's breaths, and just as the heat of a fire that has been extinguished spreads into the sky; Bhmj_14.61.
Just as the fragrance of flowers enters within the wind,
or as passion is transmitted into a porous crystal, so too does it enter.
In that same way, the self, carrying its latent impressions within, rushes toward the womb with a movement difficult to perceive,
like a wind bearing a cold touch.
For one who is born, [craving] is born; for one who grows, it grows.
Like a vine, it does not wither even as the person withers away.

Having relied upon a firm dispassion toward the conjunction with suffering through discernment, one initiated into Brahman is liberated by the mantra: "I am not; I do not exist. (Bhājana-vārttika 14.65)
First, the yogin attains nirvāṇa regarding objective entities, then regarding the functions of their causes; having reached the state of non-referentiality, he dissolves into Brahman.
Having fully realized this true state of existence, he [perceived] the Self as having hands and feet everywhere, all-pervading, and imperishable.
Having spoken thus to the brahmin, the Siddha suddenly vanished.
O son of Kuntī, listen further to this [teaching] as you strive for your own welfare.
Long ago, in a secluded place, a certain brahmin woman said to her husband:
"O virtuous one, I shall go to my destination; for what purpose am I devoted solely to you?"
Thus questioned by her, the brahmin, with a smiling face, said to her:
"The fire named Vaiśvānara indeed dwells within embodied beings."
The senses, mind, and intellect are known as the seven flames of that fire;
the objects of the senses are its fuel, and the seven enjoyers are the officiating priests.
When that [fire] is extinguished, all this world is born again and again.
Just as the senses are to the mind, so too is the mind to them;
through their mutual assistance, they find delight in their union within the body.
In former times, the seven deer of the senses, beginning with the mind and the intellect,
were slain by the King through the use of non-discursive, yoga-infused arrows.
"For one who has conquered the senses, this entire world is nothing; for one who is a slave to sense objects, it is everything. Thus did Janaka speak to the brahmin.
Therefore, having seen all this with an unattached mind, I,
who know the higher and the lower, have renounced it for the sake of pacifying the manifestation of existence.
O auspicious one, your destiny too shall always be equal to my own state;
know that the fire of knowledge has arisen from the friction-sticks of Brahman.
Having heard these words of her husband, the Brahmin woman, who perceived the truth,
attained supreme proficiency in the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field.
Having heard this, Arjuna, overwhelmed with wonder, spoke to Kṛṣṇa:
"Who was that Brahmin, the lord of yogins, and where does he dwell, as well as his wife?"
Thus addressed, the enemy of Kaiṭabha spoke again to Dhanañjaya:
"In the past, when questioned by his disciple, the omniscient Teacher spoke as follows."
This discourse on the severance of existence was heard from the Self-Existent One and proclaimed by the lords of sages, such as Bṛhaspati and others, who possess all-encompassing vision.
For living beings bound by the three qualities and subject to the transformations of various karmas, this state of being— though always small— attains the status of something not small.
This manifold creation, it is said, has emerged from the ego;
into that very same [ego] it goes to its dissolution, like a heap of flowers falling into a pit.
The ego-sense, which has become internal through practice over hundreds of previous births—by what means can it be pierced away from the mind as if in play? (Bhājana-vārttika 14.83)
For one who has gradually relinquished all actions through the attenuation of ignorance,
the light of knowledge arises upon the cessation of conceptual constructions and dualities.
Having burned the poisonous tree of worldly existence with the fully kindled fire of knowledge,
one who is liberated from all knots attains the supreme nectar.
Thus, in the past, this knowledge proclaimed by Brahmā was told by the Guru to the disciple,
endowed with various illustrations, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence.
"I alone am the teacher, O Pārtha, and you are my disciple; you are equal to me.
Having said this, Janārdana, having imparted the entirety of knowledge, became silent.
***** The Anugītā ***** Then, after having spent a very long time in joy with the Diademed One (Arjuna), Kṛṣṇa,
longing for his kinsmen, set his mind on returning to Dvārakā. Bhājaka 14.88.
Having gone there, he took leave of King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his followers,
comforted Kṛṣṇā and Kuntī, and after bowing down, took his younger sister with him.
"I shall meet you again after completing the horse sacrifice," having made this agreement,
the one whose banner is Garuḍa set forth with his chariot driven by Dāruka.
As he proceeded along the road with Sātyaki as his companion, his splendor illuminating the quarters of the sky,
the sage beheld Uttaṅka, a mass of ascetic merit.
Seeing him, Śauri bowed with reverence and, with palms joined in salutation,
inquired after the welfare of those forest-dwellers who were free from enmity.
Uttaṅka, too, having seen Hari, spoke with affection regarding his well-being: "O Bhārata, has the lineage been preserved by you through conciliation?"
I trust that King Duryodhana and the son of Dharma, along with their followers,
remain free from rivalry and established in their paternal positions through your counsel?
Thus questioned by Uttaṅka, Govinda replied to him:
"O Sage, I made the supreme effort for a reconciliation among the Bharatas."
Although he was addressed many times with beneficial advice by Vidura and others, the Kaurava did not accept it, being utterly deluded by destiny and fate.
Due to the persistence of the Kuru king, who would not turn back from his resolve, all the kings were slain; only the five Pāṇḍavas remained.
Having heard this, the sage, blazing with anger like a fire, said to him:
"Those crooked-minded ones were struck down by you yourself."
"O Kṛṣṇa, because you, though capable and desiring the welfare of Pārtha,
overlooked this terrible destruction, I therefore pronounce a curse upon you."
When Uttanka had spoken thus, the Slayer of Kaiṭabha replied:
"I know you, O Uttanka, a mass of splendor and a treasure-house of asceticism."
But you ought not, out of anger, to cause such severe waste of your ascetic merit;
for anger is unbearable and terrible darkness, the death of all embodied beings.
Even now your delusion is not destroyed; indeed, even now you do not see.
Do you not know me, who am everything, all-pervading, and immutable?
When Puṣkarākṣa had said, "I am the creator consisting of all gods, the soul of the universe, and the source of all worlds," the sage, his anger appeased, spoke.
"I know you; however, I wish to see that divine body of yours.
Thus was he entreated by the Lord of Sages, who sported in the playful manifestation of the universe.

Having beheld that divine form—which is beyond the three lights, eternal, and at the forefront of consciousness filled with the radiance of power; wherein Brahmā, Rudra, Mahendra, and Candra flash like lines—he, the best of sages, became one whose delusion was extinguished.
Then, having been honored with hymns of praise and devotion by Uttaṅka, Viṣṇu resumed that very same gentle form of his at his word.
"O Sage, I shall provide for your sustenance at all times through mere remembrance.
Having spoken thus and taken leave of him, the one whose banner is Garuḍa departed.
Then once, while wandering through desert wastes in search of water, that sage saw a Caṇḍāla, bow in hand, providing water.
Although he was entreated by him repeatedly with the words, "Take it," when the sage Utaṅka did not accept the impure water, [the serpent] then vanished.
Then the Blessed Viṣṇu himself, having approached him, said:
"O Sage, at my word Śakra has come to give you the nectar."
That Cāṇḍāla was not a water-carrier; your suspicion was false. Since you rejected him out of delusion, you have acted improperly.
"Now, by my boon, let this desert land be filled with streams of nectar-like water," saying this, Hari departed.
Thus was this Uttaṅka, a treasury of glory and possessed of great power;
he obtained a rare sight of Viṣṇu, accompanied by His grace.
Having attained supreme knowledge in the past through service to his guru, he set out for the palace of King Pauṣya, desiring to offer him the teacher’s fee.
Having obtained two beautiful earrings bestowed by his wife Pauṣā,
and seeing them stolen and lost, he descended to the underworld for the sake of his lord of life.
Having conquered the Nāgas and obtained those two jeweled earrings in former times,
he gave them to his teacher’s wife and became one who had fulfilled his purpose.
***** Uttaṅka’s Vision of Viśvarūpa ***** When Kṛṣṇa, the bestower of joy upon the Yādavas, had departed for Dvāravatī,
Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his ministers, reflected upon the requirements of the sacrifice. (Bhājana 14.117)
Having gone slowly to that mountain beloved of Śrīkaṇṭha, he, along with his younger brother,
propitiated Rudra, the god of gods, the wielder of the Pināka bow, through ascetic penance.

When the fire had been gratified by the sages and by the family priest Dhaumya,
the illustrious son of Pāṇḍu obtained the treasure deposited by Marutta.
There were thousands of golden vessels of vast proportions and diverse radiant forms, as well as hundreds of loads of jewels.
He brought ten lakhs of camels, carts, horses, and likewise elephants— that wealth— to Hastināpura.
At that time, there was no counting the buffalo-drawn carts, nor the men, nor the oxen, as they carried away vast quantities of gold.
Then, when the king had reached his own city, Madhusūdana took up an inexhaustible treasury and returned accompanied by all the Vṛṣṇis.
At that very moment, the queen of Saubhadra gave birth to a lifeless son, consumed by the weapon of Droṇa’s son.
When a son was born to Uttarā, there arose the festive sound of "A woman has given birth! which instantly became the sound of weeping: "Lifeless! Lifeless! BhmJ 14.126.
When the infant was born with limbs as tender as young shoots and buds,
yet lifeless, the motherly folk fainted from grief.
Then Kuntī and Subhadrā, having approached the ocean of compassion,
spoke to the husband of Rukmiṇī with voices choked with tears.
Today, the infant son of your beloved nephew Abhimanyu, who is the very embodiment of glory, has been born lifeless.
Hearing this, the Blessed One, the creator of all beings, moved by compassion,
entered the delivery chamber adorned with golden jars.
Tawny with the rays of radiant jewels, strewn with hundreds of glowing medicinal herbs,
and protected by mantras, physicians, fire, weapons, and missiles.
Then, having regained consciousness and being sprinkled with cold water,
she took the infant in her arms and lamented before Hara.
Then Śauri, with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud, spoke,
gazing slowly at the infant with an eye that rained down nectar.
Just as nothing is dearer to me than truth, the twice-born, and dharma,
by that truth may this child, released by the weapon, live today!
When Mādhava had spoken thus, that boy, having regained his life,
became like a lotus bud touched by the rays of the sun.
Then, as the great city festival suddenly commenced, even the sky-dwellers raised a cry of "Well done! Well done! in the air.
"Since this infant was born when the Kuru lineage had been utterly exhausted,
let him therefore be known by the name Parīkṣit," Keśava then said.

***** The Birth of Pirakṣit ***** // 4 // Then, by the command of Vyāsa, for the king, there was prepared a vast collection of materials— abounding in great wealth, rich with many jewels, and full of wonders— suitable for the sacrifice. Bhmj_14.138 //
Then, having released the black-spotted horse according to the prescribed rite—
which had been guarded by the son of Pāṇḍu himself, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow— [he departed].
At the end of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the son of Dharma became initiated;
wearing a golden garland, carrying a staff, shaven-headed, and clothed in a black antelope skin.
Then, when the sacrificial horse had reached the territory of the Trigartas,
a tumultuous battle took place between the princes and Savyasācin.
He had received Yudhiṣṭhira’s command that kings were not to be slain;
remembering that, he did not kill the monarchs, but merely conquered them.
Having defeated in battle the heroic son of Bhagadatta, Vajradatta, the lord of Prāgjyotiṣa and a warrior who fights from an elephant, within three days.
On foot in the battle, Pārtha fought for a very long time against the fierce warriors of Sindh, who were mounted upon chariots and elephants.
Then Duḥśalā, taking her young grandson, the son of Jayadratha,
approached Savyasācin and spoke with tearful eyes.
"Brother, when you arrived and merely heard your name,
my son Jayadratha went to his death, his heart shattered."
"This son of hers is my grandson, the son of your sister's daughter;
he must be protected with all your soul," saying this, the daughter of Dhṛtarāṣṭra wept.
Having consoled her as she was despondent, Pārtha, his eyes moist with tears,
followed the horse while censuring his own kṣatriya caste.
Then the king’s son, Babhruvāhana, went out to meet Śvetāśva, the protector of horses, who had arrived at the city of Maṇipūra.
Having accepted the worship and seeing his son standing before him with palms joined in reverence, the son of Śakra, desiring battle, did not welcome him.
Seeing me arrived with weapons, he asked, "Why do you come forward with conciliation? Dhananjaya said to him, "Fie on you, a coward who is no kshatriya! (Bhājana 14.151)
In the meantime, a serpent-maiden, having burst forth from the earth,
spoke to Babhruvāhana in the presence of her husband, the son of Pāṇḍu.
This father of yours, who is fond of great warriors, finds satisfaction in battle;
for those possessed of self-respect, the glory of heroism bears fruit through a lineage of heroes.
Thus addressed by her, that archer, having mounted his chariot with its golden-green banner and still wearing his armor, went forth to fight his father.
Then, though pierced by hundreds of arrows and exhausted by him, Dhanañjaya,
filled with joy, praised his prowess.
The son of Citrāṅgadā cut down with his own arrows the iron shafts, heavy as thunderbolts, released by the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, even before they had reached him.
Then the son of Śakra [Arjuna] blew away the chariot of his mother’s brother’s son,
as the wind disperses a garden variegated with creepers of golden leaves.
Beholding his son fighting without agitation though deprived of his chariot,
Vijaya discharged arrows with diminished effort and slackened aim.
Then, with a sharp feathered shaft, Babhruvāhana struck Śvetavāhana in the heart, as if splitting a mountain with a thunderbolt.
When Arjuna, who was invulnerable to all beings, was slain by his own son, a cry of "Alas! Alas! arose from the gods in the sky.
Seeing his father fallen upon the earth like the banner of Indra,
the son of Arjuna, having cast aside his bow, fainted while reproaching himself.
Then Citrāṅgadā, having approached and beheld her husband slain by her son, the slender-waisted woman, overcome with grief, lamented: Bhājana 14.162.
"O noble son! Having returned after a long time, you have at last found hospitality in my home from a son who is stronger than you. (Bhājana 14.163)
"Alas! I am truly one whose fortune is destroyed, that I behold you, my husband, who have been long away from home—the very delight of my eyes—now lying slain upon the earth."
Having spoken thus and embraced her husband firmly, Ulūpī, the daughter of the Nāgas, fell to the ground with her voice choked with tears, while Citrāṅgadā remained there.
Then, having regained consciousness, Babhruvāhana, afflicted by grief and withered by his own transgression, lamented and made a vow to renounce his body.
Then the female nāga meditated in her mind upon the life-restoring jewel; and as she meditated, that jewel came forth from the world of the nāgas.
Then, touched by him on the heart, Phalguna regained his life;
and Citrāṅgadā, suddenly casting off her grief, was overcome with shame.
Then, having related the account, Ulūpī, daughter of the serpent, spoke to Arjuna— who was like one awakened from sleep— as he stood firm with the ocean of his fortitude.
"This curse was given to you long ago by the Vasus because of the slaying of Bhīṣma;
for who else is capable of defeating you in battle, you who have already conquered Dhūrjaṭi?"
Out of affection for me, my father and those Vasus placed this great, radiant jewel upon you, saying that it would bring an end to your curse. (Bhājana-vastu 14.171)
Having heard this, Pārtha was struck with wonder; he then gently consoled the nāga woman Citrāṅgadā and accepted the worship offered by her daughter.
Then that heroic Pāṇḍava, having taken leave of his beloved son,
wandered across the earth girt by the oceans in pursuit of the horse.
Having conquered the lord of Magadha, the grandson of Jarāsandha, as well as the Vaṅgas, Puṇḍras, Kirātas, and the people of Dakṣiṇāpatha along with the Magadhas; ||| 14.174 ||
He commanded the princes of Gandhāra, the sons of Subala, who were skilled strikers: "All of you must come to the king's sacrifice. (Bhājana 14.175)
Then, honored by the citizens, the victorious Arjuna entered Hastināpura together with his horse that had returned from its journey.

***** The Hayotsarga [Sacrifice] ***** Then, when the sacrifice of the king, who showered gold, had commenced according to the rules, and all the kings had arrived, the place was crowded with hosts of sages. (Bhājana-vastu 14.177)
When Babhruvāhana had arrived with his mother before the king,
he was respectfully honored by the sons of Pāṇḍu out of affection for Phalguna.
Having prepared himself for the divine initiation that burns away all impurities without remainder,
the son of Satyavatī himself performed the rites of the great sacrifice.
There, everything— the piling of bricks and so forth, as well as the sacrificial posts, vessels, jars, bowls, couches, houses, and arches— was made of gold.
The celestial sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras sang auspicious songs,
and throngs of Apsarases danced during the intervals between the rites of the sacrifice.
When the herd of animals had been pacified, O best of Brahmins, they slaughtered the horse according to the scriptures, having bound it to the sacrificial post made of *pārṣatī* wood.
Then those priests, having extracted the omentum of the horse there and cooked it, presented the auspicious smoke to the Pāṇḍavas.
Then, when [the period] was complete according to the prescribed rite, the lord of the earth offered the earth, whose girdle is the four oceans, as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to Vyāsa.
Then, having given ten million times ten million gold pieces at the king's word,
he received back from the brahmins the earth that had been offered by the sage.
Then, after the king had honored those kings who were worthy of respect and they had been dismissed,
there arose a great festival of the assembly of Brahmins.
There were rivers of honey, milk, and ghee;
and heaps of sweetmeats, resembling the great boundary mountains, shone forth.
As gold and jewels were being bestowed upon the twice-born by the king,
the ten directions shone forth, filled with them as if with the weapons of Indra.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with Vidura, Sañjaya, and the sons of Subala,
stood there like deities, being honored by the kings.

***** The Sacrifice ***** In the meantime, a mongoose with sides variegated like gold, moving with light strides, emerged from the mouth of its burrow and approached the sacrificial ground. (Bhājana-mālā 14.190)
In a human voice, he spoke, generating wonder in the people:
"Aha! This great sacrifice is not equal to even a single handful of grain."
Surely a pure particle of a gift, though small, spreads its fame among men;
surely the possession of vast wealth is merely a hollow display of festive ostentation.
When he had spoken thus, being questioned by the brahmins who were filled with wonder, he said:
"O twice-born ones, let the greatness of the *sraktuprastha* be heard."
In ancient times, there was a twice-born man in Kurukṣetra who lived by gleaning ears of grain;
he possessed the wealth of a pure nature, yet he was emaciated and supported a large family.
Once, during a terrible famine, his means of subsistence having long since failed,
he wandered through a hundred fields with great difficulty and obtained a single measure of barley meal.
Having performed his necessary domestic duties according to the Vaiśvadeva rite,
he set out with his wife to eat, and on the way he saw a supplicant.
Overcome by hunger, that twice-born man, his heart filled with the nectar of contentment, saw his guest who was likewise overcome by hunger and gave him his own food.
When his hunger was not appeased by eating that, even though he was a seeker of food,
then his wife, his son, and his daughter-in-law gave it to him.
Then, having been satisfied by the food of all, that guest said: "I am pleased with your righteousness; may you attain great success! (Bhājana 14.199)
When he had spoken thus and vanished, all those of praiseworthy conduct, by means of celestial chariots radiant as the sun, attained heaven in their own bodies.
Then, summoned by the scent of the flour, I, who dwelt in a hole,
reached that place of leavings where that guest had eaten.
This one side of mine, touched by the water from his vessel, has become as radiant as gold, as if bathed in merit. (Bhājana 14.202)
For a very long time, my second thought was: "How might this become golden? Because of that, I have now attained the status of a lord of the earth.
Even though he wandered through the dining grounds for hundreds of thousands of twice-born men here, not even a single lovely morsel of food was obtained by him.
"Therefore, a sacrifice does not equal even a single measure of roasted barley flour.
Having said this, Nakula, possessing a variegated splendor, vanished from sight.
Thus, purity of intention is more excellent than thousands of sacrifices;
indeed, the stainlessness of the mind is declared to be the supreme Brahman.
Long ago, at Agastya’s twelve-year sacrificial session, the Brahmins foretold to one another a terrible drought that was about to occur.
Then the high-minded Agastya, a treasury of asceticism, having abandoned the sacrifice of material offerings,
performed the sacrifice of meditation with a steady mind.
He alone, endowed with all riches, omniscient, and having made his presence manifest,
became the sacrificial rite (kratu) by which Indra, filled with bliss, caused rain to fall.
The sacrifice of the Pāṇḍava Śreyas, whose being was purified, proceeded;
however, Nakula there caused an insult to his own duty.
In former times, Krodha himself, assuming the form of a dog, desiring to test Jamadagni, licked with his tongue the milk held in a vessel during a śrāddha ceremony. (Bhājana-mañjarī 14.211)
Recognizing that "this is anger," the Sage, whose eye is wisdom, did not curse him; thereupon, Krodha became terrified and trembled with agitation.
Then those ancestors, whose milk had been withheld from the śrāddha offering, became enraged and cursed him for a long time, by which their anger was transformed into the form of mongooses.
Having spoken words of contempt regarding the sacrifice of Yudhiṣṭhira himself, they set this limit for him: "You shall attain the end of your curse."

***** The Story of Nakula // 7 // ***** Thus, the noble tree of his conduct shone forth— honored by all the lords of men, nourished by the twice-born, possessing the various blossoms of his virtuous nature, rooted in the collection of sacrificial requisites for the sake of the mass of auspicious fruits, and bearing the branches of truth. Bhmj_14.215 //
Thus ends the Āśvamedhika Parva in the Bhāratamañjarī composed by Śrī Kṣemendra.
